study.title: Core training for chronic low back pain: modest pooled benefit, very mixed trials
study.evidence_note: Direct head-to-head RCT synthesis in CNLBP.
study.confidence_note: Results and methods are clearly reported in the article.
study.impact_line: Across active comparisons, experimental regimens pooled better than comparators, but heterogeneity was extreme and regimens varied widely.
summary: 15 RCTs; 693 people for pain and 677 for function.
Pain and function both favoured core training overall.
I2 was >90% for both primary outcomes.
Subgroup signals suggest 8+ weeks may matter for pain, not clearly for function.

pico.p: Adults with chronic non-specific low back pain
pico.i: Different active core muscle training regimens

limits: Very high heterogeneity across comparison types.
Primary outcomes are subjective and unblinded in many trials.
Regimens, dose and co-interventions varied widely.
Evidence base was largely Chinese and Korean trials.
study.bottom_line: In active-comparator trials, experimental regimens had better short-term pain and function on average, but extreme heterogeneity means this does not identify one best core method.

methods.design: Systematic review and meta-analysis of RCTs
methods.setting: Six databases; studies published through the search date
methods.intervention: Head-to-head comparisons of active core training regimens, including single and combined protocols
methods.follow_up: Post-intervention; some subgroup analyses by duration

results.effect: Between-group pooled difference across active comparisons
results.detail: 14 RCTs, 693 participants. Post-intervention pooled between-group effect across diverse active comparisons; I2 = 90%.
15 RCTs, 677 participants. Heterogeneity was high (I2 = 91%). The estimate is statistically significant but imprecise.
This subgroup was statistically significant; < 8 weeks was not. The subgroup difference test was not significant.

how_to_apply: Use as a broad signal, not a single preferred protocol.
Expect more consistent pain benefit with 8+ week programmes.
Be cautious about claiming one core method beats another.
Do not overread combined programmes; subgroup differences were not significant.
Match expectations to the comparator and co-interventions used in the trial.
Treat this as short-term evidence only.

grade.reason: Many included studies had allocation concealment and blinding problems.
Heterogeneity was very high for both primary outcomes (I2 > 90%).
Population, interventions and outcomes match the review question.
Pooled 95% CIs were reported and total samples were 677-693 participants.
Funnel plots were roughly symmetric and Egger tests were not significant.

clinical_significance: No MCID or smallest worthwhile change was reported in the source, so clinical importance cannot be judged against a named threshold.
Pain CI includes no effect, so a clinically meaningful benefit cannot be confirmed.
Function CI excludes no effect, but the estimate is still imprecise and highly heterogeneous.
The pooled effects may be statistically significant yet still not reliably transferable to one regimen.
comparator_fairness: Comparators were active core regimens, not no-treatment controls.
This is a fair design for relative effectiveness, not for absolute efficacy.
Dose, co-interventions and expectation were uneven across studies.
alternative_explanations: Natural recovery and regression to the mean could contribute in short trials.
Context and therapist contact may differ between regimens.
Co-interventions were common in combined arms.
Baseline differences and differential reporting could also influence the pooled effect.
spin: The abstract and conclusion mostly match the pooled primary outcomes.
The conclusion is stronger than the subgroup evidence for a superior modality.
Sling exercise is highlighted in the conclusion, but the subgroup evidence is not definitive.
fit_with_evidence: The paper cites a 2025 systematic review reporting benefit versus controls, which is broadly consistent with these pooled positive effects.
This review extends that work by comparing active regimens head-to-head.
It fits the Atlas lumbar playbook as exercise-based care, but not as proof of one best core method.
external_validity: Reasonable for adult CNLBP seen in sports physiotherapy.
Most studies were from China and Korea, so transfer to Australian practice needs caution.
Programmes were short term and varied widely, unlike many routine caseloads.
The sample is not clearly athlete-focused.
would_change_my_mind: A larger, preregistered head-to-head RCT with standardised dose and longer follow-up.
A network or direct-comparison review with lower heterogeneity and consistent superiority of one regimen.
Replication in an Australian clinical population with clear patient-relevant thresholds.

study.patient_explanation: Core exercise programmes for long-term low back pain seem to help on average, but the studies are mixed and no single version is clearly best. Longer programmes may help pain more, but the evidence is still uncertain.
open_questions: Which core regimen is best for which patient subgroup?
Does benefit persist after treatment ends?
How much of the effect is due to the added co-interventions?
key_findings: Experimental regimens pooled better for pain and function overall.
I2 was 90% for pain and 91% for function.
8+ week programmes had better pain estimates, but subgroup differences were not significant.
Combined programmes improved function, but superiority over single-modality training was not shown.
